title.en: Banks and the Magic of Finance

text.en: Navdeep has saved some money, but keeping it in a cupboard might not be safe. Rima runs a business making bamboo products and needs money to grow it. A bank connects people like them: it keeps savings safe and lends to those who need money. This chapter explores how banks work, how money grows through interest and compounding, and how to stay safe in the digital world.

Saving all your money in a cupboard might not be safe, so people deposit it in a bank. Money placed in a bank is called a deposit, and the person or business becomes a bank account holder. The bank gives a passbook, a diary-like document that records all receipts and payments. In return for keeping money, the bank pays interest, extra money added at regular intervals such as quarterly, monthly or yearly.
The bank earns by lending deposits to others. Just as banks pay interest to depositors, they charge interest from borrowers on the loans they provide. Farmers borrow money to start a small business or to expand farming. Banks do not lend all deposits; they keep reserve money. Example: if Anand deposits Rs 200 at 2 percent interest, he earns Rs 4 in a year.
At 6 percent a year on Rs 1,000 the interest is Rs 60 in year one. In year two interest is earned on the interest too, giving Rs 63.60, and it keeps growing. This is compounding: money grows on interest earned earlier. The story of the king of Ambalappuzha in Kerala and the sage: the king lost a chess game and had to place rice grains on the chessboard, doubling each square. By the 16th square it was 32,768 grains and by the 32nd square over 210 crore grains. Compounding helps savers, but it also makes loans grow bigger for borrowers, so borrowing needs care.
With many banks and financial institutions, clear rules are needed. After Independence the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) came under the Government of India and has been the central bank since 1949, the banker of banks. The RBI has the sole right to issue currency. Ancient temples also acted like financial institutions, with contracts etched on copper plates.
A cheque is a paper instrument to pay someone from your bank account: the amount is debited from your account and credited to the receiver. Debit and ATM cards let people withdraw cash and pay shops. A PIN is a secret numeric code. In 2016 the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) launched UPI, a fast and secure digital payment system. It supports cashless transactions and countries such as the UAE, France, Sri Lanka, Bhutan and Mauritius have adopted it.
A share is a small part of ownership of a company. A company, like a restaurant owner expanding, can raise money by issuing shares. The more shares you own, the higher your ownership. Shares are bought and sold at the stock exchange. A rise in share prices leads to a stock market boom.
Never share your PIN or an OTP (One-Time Password) with anyone. In case of fraud, report it through helpline 1930 or the National Cybercrime Reporting Portal.

problem.en: Rima deposits Rs 1,000 at 6 percent a year. How much interest does she earn in year one, and why is year two's interest more?

text.en: 6 percent of 1,000 = Rs 60.
In year two interest is earned on 1,060, giving Rs 63.60.

prompt.en: Explain to a friend how a bank earns money and why it pays you interest.

requiredIdeas.en: The bank lends deposits to borrowers.
Part of it is paid to depositors.

commonMisconceptions.en: Believing banks lend every rupee deposited.

points.en: Banks keep savings safe and lend money.
Interest rewards savers; borrowers pay interest.
Compounding makes money grow on earlier interest.
The RBI is the central bank; UPI began in 2016.
Never share a PIN or OTP; report fraud on 1930.
